items.title: Lesson 3, Investigate (PhysicsLAB: Emission Spectra and Finding the Size of an Atom): (1) An unknown gas shows bright lines at 447, 502, 588 and 668 nm. The reference lines are hydrogen 656, 486, 434, 410 nm; helium 447, 502, 588, 668 nm; neon 585, 640, 703 nm. Identify the gas. (2) A sheet of gold leaf is 1.0e-7 m thick and is about 350 atoms thick. Estimate the diameter of a gold atom. (Sample/expected results.)

body.html: An element's line pattern is unique, so matching all the lines identifies the gas. A thickness divided by the number of atom layers gives the size of one atom.
(1) Compare each line with the references. All four measured lines match the helium list. None of the hydrogen or neon lines match. (2) Diameter = thickness divided by number of layers:

answer.html: (1) The unknown gas is helium. (2) A gold atom is about 2.9 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> m (0.29 nm) across, close to the typical 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> m atomic size. The online lab data itself is not in the text, so these are the expected results.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Rutherford): In a gold-foil simulation, 5 of every 40,000 alpha particles bounce nearly straight back. Why would this have surprised someone who believed in the plum- pudding model, and what fraction bounces back?

body.html: In the plum-pudding model the positive charge is spread evenly through the atom.

The fraction is 5 / 40, 000 = 1.25 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup>, or 1 in 8000. With evenly spread charge, a heavy, fast alpha particle should pass through with only small deflections. Even a handful of reversals means a very strong, concentrated force somewhere in the atom.

answer.html: About 1 in 8000 reverse. The plum-pudding model predicts none, so the positive charge and most of the mass must be concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Emission spectra): A forensic lab heats a glass fragment in a flame and records the light with a spectroscope. How can the spectrum tell the lab what elements are in the glass and how much of each?

answer.html: Each element emits its own set of bright lines. Matching the lines with known spectra identifies the elements. The brighter an element's lines, the more of it is in the sample, so comparing intensities gives the relative amounts.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Stars): A glowing gas cloud (nebula) in space is seen against a dark sky. How can astronomers use its light to find what it is made of?

answer.html: A hot, thin gas cloud gives an emission spectrum. Astronomers pass its light through a spectroscope and see bright lines. They compare those lines with the known emission lines of elements to find which elements are present.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 18 question: The first four ultraviolet lines of hydrogen (Lyman series) have wavelengths of 121.6 nm, 102.6 nm, 97.3 nm and 95.0 nm. Compare the differences between adjacent wavelengths as the energy increases.

body.html: The lines are 121.6, 102.6, 97.3 and 95.0 nm. Energy increases as wavelength decreases.
Differences between neighbors: 121.6 −102.6 = 19.0 nm, 102.6 −97.3 = 5.3 nm, 97.3 −95.0 = 2.3 nm.

answer.html: As energy increases, the gaps between adjacent lines get smaller (19.0 nm, then 5.3 nm, then 2.3 nm), so the lines crowd together at the high-energy end.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 21 question: The diagram shows four possible photon emissions A, B, C and D in a hydrogen-like atom (energy levels to scale). Which transition produces the photon with the greatest energy, and which produces the longest wavelength?

body.html: 𝐸<sub>photon</sub> = 𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>−𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub> is largest for the longest arrow, and the smallest-energy photon has the longest wavelength (𝜆= ℎ𝑐/ 𝐸).

A is 𝐸<sub>4</sub> →𝐸<sub>1</sub>, B is 𝐸<sub>3</sub> →𝐸<sub>2</sub>, C is 𝐸<sub>4</sub> →𝐸<sub>3</sub> and D is 𝐸<sub>2</sub> →𝐸<sub>1</sub>. The longest arrow is A. The shortest arrow is C, whose levels are closest together.

answer.html: Transition A (𝐸<sub>4</sub> →𝐸<sub>1</sub>) gives the greatest-energy photon (shortest wavelength), and transition C ( 𝐸<sub>4</sub> →𝐸<sub>3</sub>) gives the lowest-energy photon, which has the longest wavelength.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Quantum number): By what factors do the orbital radius and the magnitude of the energy of a hydrogen electron change when it moves from 𝑛= 2 to 𝑛= 5?

body.html: 𝑟<sub>𝑛</sub>= 𝑛<sup>2</sup>𝑟<sub>1</sub>, so 𝑟<sub>5</sub> / 𝑟<sub>2</sub> = 25 / 4 = 6.25. 𝐸<sub>𝑛</sub>= −13.6 / 𝑛<sup>2</sup>, so 𝐸<sub>2</sub> = −3.40 eV and 𝐸<sub>5</sub> = −0.544 eV, a factor of 4 / 25 = 0.16 in magnitude.

answer.html: The radius grows by a factor of 6.25, and the energy rises from −3.40 eV to −0.544 eV (it becomes less negative, with a magnitude 0.16 times as large).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Hydrogen lines): Describe the transitions that give hydrogen's ultraviolet lines, and explain why they are not visible.

answer.html: Each ultraviolet line comes from an electron dropping from a higher level (𝑛= 2, 3, 4, … ) to the 𝑛= 1 level. The smallest such drop is −3.40 −( −13.6) = 10.2 eV, which is well above the 3.1 eV top of the visible range, so the photons are ultraviolet.

answer.html: 𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= −30.5 eV

items.title: Lesson 3, Physics Challenge: An atom in a krypton laser is treated as hydrogen, and an electron makes the transition 𝑛= 6 →𝑛= 4. The measured wavelength is 647.1 nm. Find (a) the photon energy predicted by the Bohr model, (b) the predicted wavelength, and (c) the percent discrepancy from the measured value.

question.html: (a) Photon energy predicted by the Bohr model

body.html: 𝑛= 6 →4; measured 𝜆= 647.1 nm.

answer.html: (b) 𝜆≈2630 nm (infrared)
(c) about 3.1 × 102%; the predicted wavelength is about four times the real one, so the Bohr model fails for atoms with many electrons.

check.html: A discrepancy this large confirms the model's limitation.

items.title: 40: A hydrogen atom in the 𝑛= 1 state is illuminated with photons of 10.2 eV, 11.5 eV and 12.1 eV. Which are absorbed? Explain using energy conservation.

body.html: An absorbed photon's energy must equal the gap between two levels, 𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= ℎ𝑓.

The gaps from 𝑛= 1 are 𝐸<sub>2</sub> −𝐸<sub>1</sub> = −3.40 −( −13.6) = 10.2 eV and 𝐸<sub>3</sub> −𝐸<sub>1</sub> = −1.51 −( −13.6) = 12.1 eV. The photons of 10.2 eV and 12.1 eV match these gaps exactly. A photon of 11.5 eV does not match any gap, so no jump can conserve energy.

answer.html: The 10.2 eV and 12.1 eV photons are absorbed (taking the atom to 𝑛= 2 and 𝑛= 3). The photon's energy goes into the atom, raising it by exactly the photon energy. The 11.5 eV photon is not absorbed.

items.title: the nucleus, and the fraction of the atom's volume that the nucleus fills.

body.html: Volume scales as radius cubed.

answer.html: The atom is about 2.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> times wider than its nucleus, and the nucleus fills only about 1.3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>13</sup> of its volume. The nucleus holds the positive charge and nearly all the mass; the atom is mostly empty space.

items.title: 42: White light passes through a cool gas whose lowest two energy levels differ by 2.10 eV, and then through a prism. Describe how to see the gas's absorption spectrum and predict where a dark line appears.

body.html: Atoms absorb photons whose energy matches a gap between levels.

answer.html: Send white light through the cool gas and then through a prism or grating. Photons of 2.10 eV (590 nm) are absorbed by atoms in the lowest level, so that wavelength is missing from the transmitted light and appears as a dark line (yellow-orange) in an otherwise continuous spectrum. It is at the same wavelength as the gas's bright emission line.

items.title: 43: Compare the light from a glowing electric-stove coil with the light from a neon sign.

answer.html: The hot coil is an incandescent solid and gives a continuous spectrum with colors that blend smoothly (mostly red and infrared at low temperature). The neon sign is an atomic gas and gives only a few bright lines at particular wavelengths unique to neon. Similar: in both, the light comes from energized atoms and can be studied with a prism or grating.

items.title: 44: The lowest-level radius of a lithium ion (Li2 + ) is 0.0177 nm. Find the radius of its third level.

body.html: The ion behaves like hydrogen, so 𝑟<sub>𝑛</sub>= 𝑛<sup>2</sup>𝑟<sub>1</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑟<sub>3</sub> = 0.159 nm

check.html: Nine times 𝑟<sub>1</sub>, the same pattern as hydrogen, and still a bit smaller than hydrogen's third level (0.48 nm) because of the larger nuclear charge.

answer.html: 𝜆≈5.9 mm (𝑓≈5.1 × 10<sup>10</sup> Hz), in the microwave region of the spectrum.

check.html: The levels are very close together at high 𝑛, so the photon energy is tiny and the wavelength is long.

items.title: 46 (Critical Thinking): Build a scale model of hydrogen using a golf ball (radius 2.1 cm) for the nucleus. The nucleus radius is 1.5 × 10−15 m and the 𝑛= 2 orbit radius is 2.1 × 10−10 m. How far from the golf ball would the 𝑛= 2 electron be?

body.html: Model nucleus radius 2.1 cm; real nucleus 1.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>15</sup> m; real 𝑛= 2 radius 2.12 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> m.
Scale every length by the same factor.

answer.html: The 𝑛= 2 electron would be about 3.0 km from the golf ball.

check.html: The ratio of orbit radius to nucleus radius is about 1.4 × 10<sup>5</sup>, so a hydrogen atom is mostly empty space.

items.title: Lesson 3, Investigate (PhysicsLAB: Emission Spectra and Finding the Size of an Atom)

body.html: These are online labs that need the lab's own data, which is not in the text.

Method for Emission Spectra: measure the wavelengths of the bright lines, compare them with the reference line patterns of known gases (as in Figure 15), and name the gas whose lines all match. Method for Finding the Size of an Atom: use the scale of the model (for example, a measured length divided by the number of atoms or the size of a particle) and scale it up or down to the real size. A representative result is an atomic diameter of about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> m (0.1 nm).

answer.html: Cannot be completed without the online lab data. The method is given above; a typical atom is about 0.1 nm across.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Rutherford): Why was Rutherford so surprised by the gold foil results?

body.html: Thomson's "plum pudding" model spread the positive charge evenly through the atom.

With evenly spread charge, a massive, fast alpha particle should pass through with only tiny deflections. Instead, about one in 20,000 bounced back at angles over 90°, which Rutherford compared to a cannon shell bouncing off tissue paper.

answer.html: He expected only slight deflections but saw a few large-angle and even backward scatterings, which meant the positive charge and mass must be concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Emission spectra): How can an emission spectrum identify the composition and concentrations of elements in a sample?

answer.html: Each element emits its own unique set of wavelengths, so matching the lines in the sample's spectrum with the known spectra of elements identifies which elements are present. The more of an element there is, the brighter its lines, so comparing line intensities gives the relative concentrations (percent composition).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Stars): Describe how scientists determine the composition of stars.

answer.html: Starlight is passed through a spectroscope. The cool gases in the star's atmosphere absorb certain wavelengths and leave dark (absorption) lines. Scientists match the missing lines with the known emission spectra of elements to see which elements are in the star (for the Sun, mostly hydrogen and helium).

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 18 question: Compare the differences between adjacent wavelengths as energy increases.

body.html: The hydrogen lines are 656 nm (red), 486 nm (green), 434 nm (blue) and 410 nm (violet). Energy increases as wavelength decreases.
Differences between neighbors: 656 −486 = 170 nm, 486 −434 = 52 nm, 434 −410 = 24 nm.

answer.html: As energy increases, the gaps between adjacent lines get smaller (170 nm, then 52 nm, then 24 nm), so the lines crowd together toward the violet end.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 21 question: Which transition produces the photon with the greatest energy?

body.html: 𝐸<sub>photon</sub> = 𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>−𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub> is the largest when the drop in energy is the largest.
Figure 21 shows 𝐸<sub>3</sub> →𝐸<sub>1</sub>, 𝐸<sub>2</sub> →𝐸<sub>1</sub> and 𝐸<sub>3</sub> →𝐸<sub>2</sub>. The biggest energy drop is from 𝐸<sub>3</sub> to 𝐸<sub>1</sub>.

answer.html: The 𝐸<sub>3</sub> →𝐸<sub>1</sub> transition (photon 1) gives the greatest-energy photon (and the shortest wavelength, 𝜆<sub>1</sub>).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Quantum number): Describe how orbital radius and energy depend on the principal quantum number.

answer.html: The orbital radius increases as 𝑛<sup>2</sup> (𝑟<sub>𝑛</sub>= 𝑛<sup>2</sup>𝑟<sub>1</sub>), so it grows quickly. The energy is 𝐸<sub>𝑛</sub>= −13.6 eV / 𝑛<sup>2</sup>, so it becomes less negative (rises toward 0) as 𝑛 increases, and the spacing between levels shrinks.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Hydrogen lines): Describe the transitions that give the visible lines of hydrogen.

answer.html: Each visible line comes from an electron dropping from a higher level (𝑛= 3, 4, 5 or 6) down to the 𝑛= 2 level. The 𝑛= 3 →2 transition is the red line, and higher starting levels give green, blue and violet.

answer.html: (b) 𝜆≈1280 nm (infrared)
(c) about 1.0 × 102% (roughly 103%); the Bohr model predicts about double the real wavelength, so it fails for multi-electron atoms.

check.html: A discrepancy of this size confirms the model's limitation.

items.title: 40: Explain how energy is conserved when an atom absorbs a photon.

answer.html: The photon disappears and its energy ℎ𝑓 goes into the atom, raising it by exactly 𝛥𝐸<sub>atom</sub> = 𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= ℎ𝑓. The total energy of photon plus atom is the same before and after.

items.title: 41: Summarize the atom in Rutherford's nuclear model.

answer.html: All the positive charge and more than 99.9 percent of the mass are packed into a tiny, dense nucleus at the center. The electrons, which have very little mass, occupy the rest of the volume (the atom is about 50,000 times wider than its nucleus), so an atom is mostly empty space.

items.title: 42: Absorption spectrum of hydrogen (Figure 24)

body.html: The figure shows a continuous rainbow with four narrow dark lines at about 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm.

answer.html: To find an absorption spectrum, send white light through a cool sample of the gas and then through a prism or diffraction grating. The hydrogen atoms absorb photons whose energies exactly match gaps between their energy levels (the 2 →3, 4, 5, 6 jumps, which are the same wavelengths as hydrogen's emission lines: 656, 486, 434 and 410 nm). Those wavelengths are missing from the transmitted light, so they show up as dark lines in an otherwise continuous spectrum.

items.title: 43: Emission spectra of incandescent solids and atomic gases

answer.html: An incandescent solid gives a continuous spectrum with all colors from red to violet. A gas gives only a few separate bright lines at particular wavelengths that are unique to the element. Similar: in both cases the light comes from heated or energized atoms, and each can be studied with a prism or diffraction grating. (A gas's line pattern also matches its absorption lines.)
